title: One camera move per clip
rule: Give each clip exactly one camera move; never stack push, pan, tilt and zoom.
why: Stacked or contradictory moves make the model split effort and produce unstable, warped output. Vendors Kling, Luma, Runway and OpenAI all say so.
how: Camera: slow push-in, one continuous shot. Not: push in, then pan and tilt up.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js SCENES_SYSTEM (cam: ONE continuous camera move); public/js/wizard-model.js oneMove, composeClip

title: Strip sequence words from the camera line
rule: Remove "then", "cut to", "followed by", "reveals" and similar from every camera line; keep only the first move.
why: Sequence words read as a new beat or viewpoint and the generator inserts a cut; MiniMax H3 shows this in Monofilm tests.
how: oneMove("close on hands, then her face") returns "close on hands".

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js oneMove

title: Ask for a continuous shot, but do not trust it
rule: Add an explicit "one continuous shot, no cuts" cue, and still check the result for cuts.
why: The cue helps but is not a guarantee; fixes are fewer beats, one location, one action and one camera behaviour.
how: Camera: fixed medium-wide, one continuous shot. Then review and regenerate when a cut appears.

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js composeClip (one continuous shot; No scene change, no cuts)

title: Always give the move a speed word
rule: Put a pacing word (slow, steady, gradual, creeping) next to every camera move and avoid fast moves.
why: Without a speed word the move is generic; fast moves cause warping and spatial artifacts. The same orbit reads calm or frantic by speed alone.
how: Camera: slow, steady push-in over the whole clip.

monofilm.where: normalizeCamera in public/js/wizard-model.js adds a speed word to every move

title: Say "camera holds still" when you want it still
rule: For a static shot state it positively ("Camera holds completely static", "locked viewpoint"), and put it at the start where the model is known to drift.
why: Many models drift the camera slightly by default; negative phrasing ("no camera movement") can produce movement.
how: Locked-off medium shot, camera holds completely static, she turns toward the window.

monofilm.where: normalizeCamera says "the camera holds still" for a static shot

title: Image-to-video prompts describe change, not content
rule: When a start picture is given, the prompt names only motion, camera and scene response; never restate what the picture shows.
why: The picture fixes appearance; extra words that disagree with it make the model flip between the two and waste prompt space.
how: Start picture + "She lifts the cup. Camera: slow push-in." Not a re-description of her coat.

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js composeClip (Characters ... look exactly as in the start picture)

title: Only ask for motion the picture supports
rule: Every action in a clip must be possible from the start picture: nothing needing unseen body parts, nothing outside the frame, nothing that contradicts the picture state.
why: Unsupportable motion is ignored or degraded by the model.
how: Check the move list against the start picture before export.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js SCENES_SYSTEM (every action must already be physically possible at that moment)
monofilm.idea: Add a review check that compares each clip move with its start-state sentence.

title: One action per clip and 4 to 8 seconds
rule: Plan one clear subject action per clip and keep clips between 4 and 8 seconds, splitting long scenes into several clips.
why: Models follow instructions more reliably in shorter clips; consistency drifts beyond about 5 to 10 s; sequential actions give inconsistent results.
how: A 12 s scene becomes two 6 s clips chained start-to-end.

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js clipPlan (MAX_CLIP), GENERATORS max_seconds 8; SCENES_SYSTEM moves per clip

title: Move limits per clip: small angles, one subject speed
rule: Keep pans under about 30 to 45 degrees, orbits around 30 degrees (never above 45), and match tracking speed to the subject.
why: Wide arcs and 360-degree orbits break geometry in a 5 s clip; one site reports usable moves 79% of the time when such mistakes are avoided (its own unreplicated figure).
how: Camera: slow orbit of about 30 degrees around the seated figure.

monofilm.idea: Add limits for orbit/pan to the generator profile and the scene writer prompt.

title: Give dollies and pull-backs depth to work with
rule: Use a dolly or pull-back only when the frame has foreground, midground and background (or a clear reveal), and a push-in only on a subject that is mostly still.
why: Without depth a dolly reads as a zoom; a pull-back needs something to reveal; push-ins on fast subjects are hard to control.
how: Pull-back from the seed in her paw to reveal the whole garden.

monofilm.idea: Let the scene writer pick static or push-in when the subject moves fast.

title: Camera first, with shot size named
rule: Start the camera sentence with shot size, angle and movement, then subject, action, light, style.
why: Veo reads structure literally so early words weigh more; several guides put framing first because other terms modify it.
how: Medium close-up, eye level, slow push-in: a fox looks up from the soil.

monofilm.where: composeClip puts Camera after the action and mood lines
monofilm.idea: Move the shot size and angle to the front of the exported prompt and store shot size per scene.

title: Pair a lens term with a depth-of-field term
rule: When you want a look, name focal length and focus together ("85 mm, shallow depth of field") and drop the empty word "cinematic".
why: Focal length sets framing and compression, depth of field sets blur; generic words carry no instruction.
how: Slow push-in, 85 mm look, shallow depth of field.

monofilm.idea: Add an optional lens line to notes.cam or to the film look; test per generator.

title: Name the light source, direction and quality
rule: Describe light by source, direction, quality and colour ("soft window light from camera-left, warm"), never just "cinematic lighting".
why: The model decides light itself when given a mood word; concrete sources give a target.
how: Soft window light from camera-left with a warm lamp fill, cool edge light.

monofilm.where: states[] sentences carry "the light and time of day" (SCENES_SYSTEM); look.look
monofilm.idea: Add a structured light field (source, direction, colour) per place.

title: Lock one lighting phrase per scene and reuse it word for word
rule: Write the light once for a scene or place and paste the identical wording in every clip and picture prompt of it.
why: Each clip is a stateless generation; rewording "warm lamp light" to "amber glow" causes real drift.
how: Keep a lighting slot in the prompt template and record source, direction, Kelvin in the scene plan.

monofilm.where: composeClip Look line (medium, colours, exposure and time of day stay the same); scene time field
monofilm.idea: Store a per-place light phrase and inject it unchanged into every clip and frame prompt.

title: Light the widest picture first and reuse it as the reference
rule: Approve the wide frame of a scene first; draw close frames and the next scene start from it as a reference image.
why: A reference frame carries light and colour across cuts better than text; rewriting the prompt does not repair drift.
how: Next-scene start picture is drawn with the previous last picture as an anchor.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFrame (previous-scene anchor: match the light, colours and time of day; end picture made from the picture before)
monofilm.idea: Draw the scene's wide frame first and use it for closer frames.

title: Bridge big lighting jumps with an intermediate clip or a cutaway
rule: When two clips differ strongly in light (bright outside, dark inside), insert a bridging clip or a cutaway, and grade the finished film to one look.
why: A direct cut across a big light change shows as a continuity error.
how: Door-closing insert between the exterior and the interior clip.

monofilm.idea: Flag adjacent scenes whose time field differs and suggest an insert.

title: Open a scene wide, then move in
rule: Start a scene or a new place with a wide or establishing frame, then go to medium and close shots; alternate wide and close for rhythm.
why: The establishing shot gives geography and tone; random size jumps feel disjointed.
how: Scene 1 clip 1: wide, camera holds static. Later clips: medium, then close-up.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js SCENES_SYSTEM: a scene in a new place opens wide
monofilm.idea: Check it in the continuity review

title: Keep screen direction and the 180-degree line across scenes
rule: Record who is on which side of frame and which way anyone moves; keep the camera on one side of that line between cuts.
why: Crossing the line flips left and right and makes a subject seem to reverse direction.
how: cont: Mimi enters frame-left to frame-right; next scene she keeps moving left to right.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js SCENES_SYSTEM: keep screen direction state to state
monofilm.idea: Check screen direction across scenes in the continuity review

title: Match eyelines and size in shot-reverse-shot
rule: For two speakers, face them in opposite screen directions and match shot size, lens and depth of field between the two setups.
why: Matching setups read as one conversation; mismatch distracts.
how: Both over-the-shoulder, 50 mm look, A looks frame-right, B looks frame-left.

monofilm.idea: Plan dialogue scenes as paired start pictures sharing look and size.

title: Know the weak shot types
rule: Treat over-the-shoulder, POV, multi-character contact and dense fast cuts as high-risk and plan extra takes or other coverage.
why: Reporting shows these fail most often; wording rarely fixes them.
how: Budget about three generations per usable clip.

monofilm.where: SCENES_SYSTEM avoids fiddly paw work on tiny objects; retry count in studio
monofilm.idea: Add a risk flag for these shot types in the scene plan.

title: Cut on motion, not on a still frame
rule: At each seam choose an edit point where both clips are moving and put strong action opposite the weak area.
why: Motion hides small colour or lighting differences; still frames expose them.
how: Trim the first 2 frames of a clip, cut during the turn of the head.

monofilm.where: get_clip and clip.json carry assembly.cut_on_motion
monofilm.idea: Trim automatically when the film is assembled

title: Trim the first and last frames of every clip
rule: Remove the first two or three frames and the last frames of each generation before assembling.
why: First frames of extended or chained clips often contain artifacts.
how: Set in-point at frame 3.

monofilm.where: scripts/assemble-film.mjs trims the first frames of a continued clip and a frozen tail

title: Generate in the final aspect ratio
rule: Choose the delivery ratio first, draw start pictures in it, and generate the video in it; do not crop afterwards.
why: Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 discards about 68% of horizontal pixels and changes composition; a mismatched start image makes the model invent edges.
how: Film look aspect 9:16 drives both pictures and clip text.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFrame (aspect from film look); composeClip Look line

title: Vary clip length around a 4 to 6 second baseline, and frame clearly when cutting fast
rule: Use roughly 4 to 6 s per shot as the default, shorter for tension and longer for calm, and keep framing clear if cuts are fast.
why: Deviation from the baseline shapes mood; fast cutting works only when the eye knows where to look.
how: Hook scene 2 to 3 s clips, quiet scene 6 to 8 s.

monofilm.where: clipPlan splits evenly up to MAX_CLIP; scene seconds set by the scene writer
monofilm.idea: Let the scene writer tag pace and pick clip length from mood.

title: Phrase guards positively for models without a negative input
rule: Say what should happen ("camera holds static") rather than lists of "no" items; if the model has no negative input, append a short "Do not show" line only for real failures.
why: Runway-style models do not support negative phrasing; another source recommends stating exclusions to stop drift.
how: See the conflict: both are kept.

monofilm.where: forGenerator adds "Do not show: ..." for generators without a negative field; composeClip adds "No scene change, no cuts"

title: Exclusions (negative prompts) stop drift toward defaults
rule: Keep an explicit exclusion list per film (forbidden looks and things) and send it where the model accepts a negative input.
why: One source says models drift to defaults unless told what not to show; the Runway-side sources advise against negatives.
how: look.forbidden becomes "no X" entries.

monofilm.where: composeClip never list from notes.never and look.forbidden; forGenerator

title: Chain clips with the last frame and write the next as a continuation
rule: Start each clip from the end picture of the one before and say what the previous clip ended on, so the shot size, light and place carry on.
why: The last frame is the strongest anchor for light, colour and place across a seam.
how: "The clip before ended on: ... Do not repeat it."

monofilm.where: composeClip (end picture / continue from last picture); makeFrame previous-frame anchor

title: Prefer physical transitions for a long take
rule: If a take must change place without a cut, use a physical hand-off (doorway, corner, fog, focus shift) and state it.
why: These transitions work more reliably than one environment morphing into another.
how: Camera glides through the doorway; the room beyond is the kitchen.

monofilm.idea: Only if the studio adds long-take scenes; today scenes cut between places.

title: Test one variable at a time and keep a log
rule: When a camera result is wrong, change one thing (camera line, action, picture), keep a short log of version and result.
why: Changing several things hides which change helped; Runway advises simplifying the prompt before touching the picture.
how: Retry: same picture, shorter prompt; only then redraw the picture.

monofilm.where: studio retry count per scene (commit 1c6149c)
monofilm.idea: Offer a one-click simplified retry that changes only the camera line.

title: Lock the camera with a positive block, invariants and a single clear phrase
rule: For a static shot start the prompt with one positive lock phrase (locked tripod, fixed camera), say the background stays static and the character's size stays constant, and keep camera-energy words out.
why: Vendors and users agree that a prompt alone may not hold a camera still: models add a slight push-in or pan unless told; negative-only phrasing often has the opposite effect; stacking 'stable, still, smooth' dilutes the instruction. None of the sources measures it.
how: Example: 'Locked tripod shot, the camera and background stay fixed, the snail keeps the same size, it glides to the left.' Check first, middle and last frames at the same size: a growing head with the edges moving out is a zoom; bent lines with fixed anchors is background warp.

monofilm.where: forGenerator in public/js/wizard-model.js: "static, locked-off, the camera holds still... every character keeps the same size and the background stays fixed"

title: Where a generator reshapes the scene on camera moves, move the camera in post
rule: For a generator that cannot separate camera from object motion, ask for a static camera in every clip and make any push-in or pan as a uniform crop and scale of the finished clip.
why: Temporal attention links the same pixel positions, so large camera shifts break consistency; text-only and trajectory-only control entangle camera and object motion; practitioners see the subject grow when a zoom prompt is aggressive. A crop scales every part of the picture together.
how: Keep generator profile flag static_camera; in assembly, apply a slow scale (a suggested 3-8%, not from a source) with a fixed centre on the joined clip where the story wants a push-in. Camera-conditioned models (CameraCtrl, CamI2V, Direct-a-Video) exist for the case where real camera motion is needed.

monofilm.where: a push-in the generator cannot make is kept as notes.post and cropped in by scripts/assemble-film.mjs, carried through a chain of clips without a jump

title: Expect image-to-video to under-move; write a change with a target, not a mood
rule: When a slow motion barely happens, write the action as a start state to an end state with committed verbs and a distance, and use the generator's own motion setting if it has one.
why: I2V clips are more static than text-to-video because later frames over-attend to the reference frame (DyMoS lifts dynamic degree 51.7 to 64.8 on Wan 2.2 and flow about 30%); 4-step LoRAs give a slow-motion look (a node adds 15-50%); low-commitment words give a wiggle.
how: 'The snail glides one body length to the right, then stops' beats 'moves slowly'; one action per clip. Seedance has camera_fixed; with a local Wan-class sampler consider a motion gain of 1.0-1.5. Pick the best of several takes.

monofilm.where: field notes: snail barely glides; end holds of 1-4 s; trimmed in assembly
monofilm.idea: Say distance and end state in the clip prompt; test a motion gain in the local generation script.

title: A cut is the default; any other transition must carry a meaning
rule: Join shots with a hard cut when the next shot is a continuation; use a dissolve, fade or wipe only to say time, place or mood changed, and then make it long enough to be read as chosen.
why: An unmotivated hard cut at a scene change reads as a smash cut: an abrupt, jarring break, which is a device for comedy or shock, not a neutral change of place.
how: Test: strip all transitions, add back only those with a purpose; if a transition draws more attention than the moment, use a sound-led cut instead.

monofilm.where: scripts/assemble-film.mjs sceneJoin: continuing clips keep the best-frame join; a new scene always gets a dissolve or a dip
monofilm.idea: Scene changes get a dissolve or fade (see cin-p-034); clips continuing in one scene stay hard cuts.

title: Size a dissolve by the time or place it covers
rule: Use about 0.3 to 0.5 s (8 to 12 frames) to soften a cut between similar pictures, 1 to 2 s (24 to 48 frames) for a scene change in place or time, and longer only for a large time jump or a slow mood.
why: Sources agree on the 24 to 48 frame traditional range and on 6 to 12 frames as a cut softener; below that it reads as a cut, far above it as dreamlike or as an error.
how: At 24 fps: 10 frames for same-scene mismatch, 24 to 36 frames for a new scene, 48 frames for a time jump. Centre it on the cut so each clip needs half the length as handle.

monofilm.where: sceneJoin: dissolve 0.9 s, dip 1.2 s (plan.sceneDissolve, plan.sceneDip); the research range is 1.0 to 1.5 s, tune by ear
monofilm.idea: Use 1.0 to 1.5 s dissolves (xfade=dissolve or fade) at scene changes.

title: Fade through black or white only for a major break
rule: Reserve a fade out and in (dip to black) for the end of a film, a chapter or a large time jump, and a dip to white for hope or disorientation; do not use it inside a continuous scene.
why: A fade goes to a blank image instead of another shot, so it reads as an ending; used often it makes each scene feel finished.
how: xfade=fadeblack or fadewhite at 0.8 to 1.5 s; first clip fade in from black 0.5 to 1 s; last clip fade out 1 to 2 s.

monofilm.where: sceneJoin picks xfade fadeblack when the mean brightness differs by more than 30 of 255 or the pictures differ by more than 70; the film fades in over 0.6 s and out over 1.2 s (sound a little longer)
monofilm.idea: Fade in the first clip and out the last (picture and sound).

title: Make the two pictures agree before dissolving across them
rule: Before a dissolve check that subject position, framing and brightness of the last and first frames are close; if they are not, change the pictures, not the transition length.
why: A dissolve between pictures with the subject in different places shows two ghost subjects; the dissolve calls attention to the edit. A graphic or match cut works because shape, colour or position line up.
how: Prefer an end picture and next start picture that share screen position (a match dissolve, as in Citizen Kane's window), or a dip through black when they cannot.

monofilm.where: join matching by best frame inside one scene
monofilm.idea: Between scenes, choose the next scene's first picture to share the previous end picture's main shape and brightness, or dip through black.

title: Let sound lead or trail the picture at a scene change
rule: At a scene change start the next scene's sound before its picture (J-cut, pre-lap) or let the old scene's sound run on past it (L-cut); lead 6 to 15 frames (0.25 to 0.6 s) for a smooth join, up to about 2 s into a big sequence.
why: A split edit hides the seam because the ear already knows where the story goes when the eye gets there. Sources give 0.5 s for dialogue and about 2 s for a major sequence; the 6 to 15 frame figure is one editor's rule.
how: Cut the picture where it is; slide the audio of the incoming clip earlier by 0.3 to 0.6 s under a short crossfade. For a trailer-like film, 1 to 2 s lead into the first clip of a new scene.

monofilm.where: assemble-film.mjs audioGraph: at a new scene the sound of the scene before lingers 0.5 s under the new picture (an L-cut; the sound after the cut point of a clip exists). A J-cut needs sound before a clip starts, which a generated clip does not have
monofilm.idea: Offset the audio crossfade: the next clip's audio starts 0.3 to 0.6 s before its picture at scene changes.

title: Carry a music bed or ambience across a scene change
rule: Start a music cue before the cut, or let the old cue run into the new scene, and bring the new place's ambience in early; do not restart music at the cut.
why: A bridge keeps mood and continuity through a location or time change; ambience heard through a whole scene makes separate shots read as one place. Music that restarts exactly at the cut announces the cut.
how: One continuous bed under the whole film, or an overlap of 1 to 2 s between cues under a crossfade; new ambience fades in under the last second of the old shot.

monofilm.where: plan.music lays a bed under the film and ducks it under the clips (MUSIC=file scripts/film-plan.py); the studio does not make music itself, no music generator is connected
monofilm.idea: Put one music bed under the film and treat generated clip sound as ambience (wf-p-029).

title: Never leave the soundtrack dead under a cut
rule: Keep ambience or room tone under every edit and use a short crossfade at each audio join, so the join has neither a click nor a drop to digital silence.
why: A track that goes dead sounds like a failure; presence intercut under edits hides sound seams.
how: Fill gaps with the clip's own quiet tone or a looped ambience bed; crossfade 0.1 to 0.5 s for continuing clips, longer at scene changes.

monofilm.where: audioGraph: a brown-noise room tone at -46 dB under the whole film, so a join is never silent
monofilm.idea: Loop a room-tone bed under all joins; make fades longer than 0.08 s where ambience differs.

title: Choose an equal-power audio crossfade for unrelated sounds
rule: Cross two unrelated sounds with an equal-power (constant power) curve; a linear crossfade dips by about 3 dB at the middle.
why: Equal power keeps both signals near 0.707 at the midpoint so loudness stays steady; Premiere's default audio crossfade is constant power, 1 s. Linear is safer for the same sound recorded twice.
how: ffmpeg: acrossfade=d=0.5:c1=qsin:c2=qsin (quarter-sine curves; the pairing as equal-power is our inference, to be listened to).

monofilm.where: acrossfade with c1=qsin c2=qsin at every soft join
monofilm.idea: Use acrossfade with qsin curves for scene joins.

title: In a teaser, put the sound accent on the cut and leave room around it
rule: Mark each scene change on the timeline, put the hit or whoosh on it, land a riser's peak on the hit, drop out briefly before the biggest one, and duck the bed under each hit.
why: Trailers use impacts and silence to make a seam look intended; a hit on every cut loses its effect.
how: Hit 0 to 2 frames before the picture change; riser 1 to 3 s; 0.25 to 1 s of near silence before the final hit; duck bed with sidechaincompress.

monofilm.where: no sound design layer
monofilm.idea: Optional: one short impact or whoosh at scene changes of a teaser, never on every cut.

title: Hide a scene change in motion or in a matched shape
rule: Cut at peak motion (whip pan, push, object crossing the frame) or between two pictures that share a shape, colour or screen position; when in doubt serve emotion and story before spatial continuity.
why: Motion blur and a matched shape give the eye a reason to move; Murch ranks emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10% above eye-trace and space.
how: Generate the last clip of a scene ending in a camera move or a foreground passing the lens, and the next scene opening on a move in the same direction; then cut or dissolve 6 to 12 frames.

monofilm.where: scene changes are plain cuts between unrelated pictures
monofilm.idea: Prompt a motion exit and a motion entry for scene changes.
